title: Process the scheduled window—not whatever time the worker wakes up
goal: Anchor an hourly pipeline to explicit interval boundaries so queue delay, retry, and repair do not move the data window.
tag: Certification cycle 1 · focused lesson 1 · orchestration and task runtime context
concept:
A train ticket says 10:00 even when the train reaches the platform at 10:07. If a report uses 10:07 as its boundary, seven minutes of data move into a different run.

A scheduler answers which interval owns the data. Compute startup answers only when this attempt began. Keep those clocks separate. Pass an explicit half-open window such as [09:00, 10:00) into the transform, persist it with the run, and reuse it on retry.
example: The hourly payments job is scheduled for 10:00 but starts at 10:07. It must still read events with event_time >= 09:00 and event_time < 10:00. A retry at 10:19 uses the same pair. Using CURRENT_TIMESTAMP would silently change ownership.

use_case.when: Use explicit scheduled intervals for incremental jobs whose compute can queue, retry, repair, or run late.
use_case.example: An hourly payments aggregation starts seven minutes late on shared compute but must publish the same 09:00–10:00 business window.
use_case.decision: Prefer source offsets or watermarks when they define completeness better than time. For schedule-owned batches, use half-open boundaries and a durable run identity. Do not treat a default parameter as a security control.

practice: Move the actual start and retry time. Predict which timestamps belong to the 10:00 run when the scheduled window stays fixed.
boundary: The local Python and JavaScript models compare synthetic timestamps. They do not execute Lakeflow Jobs, Snowflake tasks, SQL warehouses, retries, daylight-saving transitions, watermarks, late-data correction, time zones, permissions, or billing.

10:00, the scheduled boundary
10:07, the worker start
The time the query finishes
Compute delay must not redefine the business interval.
Why use a half-open interval [09:00,10:00)?

It makes late data impossible
It removes the need for a run identifier

title: Cancelling the CompletableFuture does not interrupt its worker
goal: Separate a CompletableFuture's cancelled state from the lifecycle of work already running underneath it.
concept:
Crossing a delivery off your tracking app does not stop the van already driving down the road.

CompletableFuture.cancel(true) completes that future exceptionally with CancellationException. For this implementation, the mayInterruptIfRunning argument has no effect because interruption does not control the processing. If you need the underlying work to stop, design cooperative cancellation or own the executor task explicitly.

// Java 25 API behavior; illustrative snippet
boolean changed = future.cancel(true);
// future is cancelled; worker shutdown is a separate concern
example: Request r-52 starts a three-step report. The caller cancels the future after step one. Observers of the future receive cancellation, but the worker can still write steps two and three unless the operation checks a separate stop signal or the owner cancels a task type that supports interruption.

use_case.when: Use this distinction when timeouts, client disconnects, or hedging cancel a CompletableFuture whose work may update state or consume scarce capacity.
use_case.example: An API timeout cancels its response future while a report query continues using a database connection.
use_case.decision: For pure computations, tolerate harmless late completion when bounded. For expensive or side-effecting work, pass a cooperative cancellation token, enforce downstream deadlines, or keep the underlying Future/handle. Do not assume cancel(true) proves the effect stopped.

practice: Cancel the visible future and toggle whether the worker checks a stop flag. Predict which steps still execute.
boundary: The recorded Java example models documented CompletableFuture state transitions with integers; it does not launch a real executor task, deliver interrupts, model races, propagate deadlines, close database calls, or prove that any specific library cooperates with cancellation.

→

→

';};cancelCoop.onchange=paintCancel;cancelAfter.onchange=paintCancel;paintCancel();

The CompletableFuture moved to a cancelled exceptional state
The database query was interrupted
Every side effect rolled back
The method changes the future's state; it does not prove underlying work stopped.
Why add cooperative cancellation?
The operation can check a shared stop condition at safe boundaries
It makes every blocking library interruptible
It converts cancellation into a transaction
The worker needs its own mechanism to observe and honor the request.
What is the boundary for side effects?
Effects committed before or after visible cancellation need their own consistency design
Cancellation automatically compensates them

title: A migration ends when the old path is unused—not when the new path launches
goal: Define exit evidence for a platform migration and decommission the legacy path without mistaking deployment for adoption.
concept:
Opening a new bridge does not remove traffic from the old bridge. Drivers may keep using the familiar route for years.

A platform migration has two finish lines: the target works, and the source is no longer needed. The second needs evidence—remaining callers, traffic, data dependencies, exception owners, controlled shutdown, rollback window, and cost removal. Otherwise the organization pays for two platforms and inherits two failure surfaces.
example: The new Airflow service runs 4,800 of 5,000 workflows. The launch slide says “96% migrated,” but 200 workflows still call the old scheduler and 40 have no owner. The migration cannot close until those callers move, receive an explicit retained exception, or are retired—and the old endpoint survives a controlled stop test.

use_case.when: Use explicit exit criteria when replacing a scheduler, data platform, API, identity system, or shared library across many teams.
use_case.example: Move 5,000 workflows from Step Functions wrappers to Airflow while tracking the remaining callers and decommissioning the old control plane.
use_case.decision: Keep a temporary bridge when it reduces migration risk, but give it an owner, expiry, and usage telemetry. Close only after inbound use is understood, data is preserved, support is ready, and a controlled stop demonstrates the old path is no longer required.

practice: Change migrated, exception, and ownerless counts. Predict whether the program is launched, adoptable, or safe to decommission.
boundary: The model counts synthetic workflows. It does not discover real dependencies, prove data retention, model hidden batch callers, execute a controlled stop, estimate regulatory obligations, calculate migration cost, or authorize decommissioning.

title: A tool error teaches the model; a protocol error talks to the host
goal: Route MCP failures to the audience that can act: model-visible tool results or host-visible JSON-RPC errors.
tag: GenAI harness engineering · MCP error channels
concept:
If a cashier says “that item is unavailable; choose another,” you can recover. If the card terminal cannot parse the payment message, the store's software—not you—must repair the protocol.

In MCP, a recoverable tool failure is an ordinary tools/call result with isError: true. The model reads its text and can revise the next call. A protocol error is a JSON-RPC error handled by the host application; the model does not see it. Choose by audience, not by how severe the failure feels.
example: The model calls read-note(id="drafts"), but only welcome exists. Return isError: true with “Known ids: welcome,” so the model can retry. If a host sends malformed parameters to resources/read, return a protocol error such as invalid params so client code handles it.

use_case.when: Use explicit error channels when building MCP servers or harness adapters that must support model recovery and host diagnostics.
use_case.example: A data-quality tool cannot find rule set drafts but can tell the model which rule-set handles exist.
use_case.decision: Put actionable domain and transient tool failures in model-visible text with isError. Reserve protocol errors for host-driven resource, prompt, completion, capability, or wire failures. Scrub secrets from both channels.

practice: Choose the request type and failure. Predict whether the model, host, or neither receives actionable recovery text.
boundary: The model routes synthetic error objects. It does not start an MCP server, validate JSON-RPC, run the TypeScript SDK, exercise URL elicitation, serialize content blocks, enforce capabilities, redact secrets, retry tools, or prove host UI behavior.

title: Give the reasoner a crystal structure—not a prose description alone
goal: Understand a newly published bridge between atomistic representations and language reasoning without treating benchmarks as autonomous discovery.
tag: Technology breakthroughs · new peer-reviewed research · November 12, 2026
concept:
A building inspector needs the blueprint, not only a sentence saying “the house has three rooms.” The sentence loses distances, connections, and geometry.

A new peer-reviewed paper introduces a Large Language and Atomic Model (LLAM). A lightweight cross-modal bridge aligns an atomistic representation of a crystal with a language embedding space. The system can condition property prediction and later reasoning on structure rather than only a text summary. The paper reports benchmark and case-study improvements; it does not establish autonomous laboratory discovery.
example: Consider two crystals described with the same formula but different atomic arrangements. A text-only prompt may collapse them into the same description. A structure encoder can preserve positions and neighborhoods, while the language component explains how a predicted property influences a screening decision. The local world below only demonstrates which information channels are present.

use_case.when: Study this approach when evaluating AI systems that must combine numerical structure-property prediction with human-readable materials reasoning.
use_case.example: Screen solid electrolytes by grounding a predicted conductivity signal in a crystal representation, then generate a reviewable explanation for a scientist.
use_case.decision: Treat it as research evidence. Require external benchmark replication, uncertainty calibration, out-of-distribution tests, ablations, compute-cost analysis, and experimental validation before discovery-pipeline claims.

practice: Turn the structure bridge and numerical predictor on or off. Predict what information the reasoner can legitimately use.

title: Artifact retention is a countdown—not durable storage
goal: Set GitHub Actions artifact retention deliberately and keep deployment records in a system designed to outlive the run.
tag: CI/CD & GitHub Actions · artifacts and retention
concept:
A hotel luggage room holds your bag until checkout. It is useful handoff storage, not an archive.

A GitHub Actions artifact stores build output, test evidence, or logs for a limited retention period. A workflow can request retention-days, but it cannot exceed the repository, organization, or enterprise limit. When the artifact expires or is deleted, a later deployment cannot download it. Durable release provenance needs a longer-lived registry or record system.
example: Build sha-52 uploads dist.zip for 5 days. A production promotion waits 8 days. The workflow run is still visible, but the artifact has expired. The safe design publishes the immutable release to a package/container registry and treats the short-lived artifact as CI handoff evidence.

use_case.when: Use workflow artifacts for bounded handoff between jobs, debugging, test reports, and short review windows.
use_case.example: Keep a Spark integration-test report for 14 days while publishing the deployable image by digest to ECR.
use_case.decision: Choose retention from the consumer's maximum delay and organizational limit. Use a package, container, evidence, or records system for durable releases and compliance—not an expired workflow artifact.

practice: Change requested retention, repository limit, and promotion age. Predict whether the artifact still exists and where the durable release should live.
boundary: The model compares integer days. It does not call GitHub, upload files, calculate billing, model legal holds, validate action versions, protect artifact integrity, enforce repository settings, sign releases, or prove registry durability.

title: Retry-After says when—not whether a replay is safe
goal: Use Retry-After as scheduling guidance while keeping replay safety tied to HTTP method and application idempotency.
concept:
A shop sign saying “back in 10 minutes” tells you when to return. It does not say the cashier forgot the payment you already made.

Retry-After can tell a client how long to wait, notably with 503 and optionally 429. It does not make a non-idempotent operation safe to replay. A POST that might already have created an order still needs an idempotency key, a status lookup, or human reconciliation.
example: POST /orders with key k-52 receives 503 Retry-After: 30. The client waits 30 seconds and retries with the same key. The server returns the stored result if the first attempt committed. Without the key, waiting changes timing but not duplicate risk.

use_case.when: Use Retry-After when overload, maintenance, or rate limiting has a meaningful recovery horizon that clients should respect.
use_case.example: An order API sheds load with 503 and asks SDK clients to wait 30 seconds before a bounded retry.
use_case.decision: Retry safe/idempotent methods according to policy. For POST or side-effecting calls, require an idempotency contract or status reconciliation. Add jitter, deadlines, attempt limits, and a retry budget; never let every client wake simultaneously.

practice: Choose method, idempotency key, and response. Predict whether the client should wait, retry, reconcile, or stop.
boundary: The model uses deterministic counters. It does not send HTTP, parse dates, compensate for clock skew, implement rate limits, add jitter, coordinate clients, enforce idempotency storage, model ambiguous transport failures, or guarantee that an upstream recovers on time.

The server resolves the repeated intent to its stored result.
Replay safety comes from the idempotency contract, not the header.

walkthrough.limit: The model uses deterministic counters. It does not send HTTP, parse dates, compensate for clock skew, implement rate limits, add jitter, coordinate clients, enforce idempotency storage, model ambiguous transport failures, or guarantee that an upstream recovers on time.

sources: IETF standard; published June 2022; checked November 12, 2026
IETF standard defining 429; published April 2012; checked November 12, 2026
visual_explanation: A response splits into two independent decisions: a countdown controls when, while method and idempotency state control whether replay is safe.
written_questions: Which POST retry path currently treats Retry-After as duplicate protection?
Where is the idempotency record stored, and how long must it outlive client retries?
